ML Abstractions, Optimization,
and Gradient Descent

From four levels of abstraction to convexity, step-size dynamics, and the geometry of ill-conditioned loss surfaces.

Learning Objectives

  • Identify the four abstraction levels of ML—application, model, optimization problem, optimization algorithm—and explain why changes cascade downward.
  • Classify ML tasks as supervised classification, regression, clustering, or dimensionality reduction, and match each to appropriate algorithms.
  • Define capacity, relate it to model complexity, and use it to diagnose overfitting and underfitting.
  • Formally define convex functions and state the three-case structure of minima for continuous convex functions on closed convex domains.
  • Define global and local minima, explain why global minima are attainable for convex objectives, and give a counterexample for non-convex ones.
  • Derive the gradient-descent update rule, state conditions under which it converges, and explain how step size causes divergence or slow convergence.
  • Define the condition number of the Hessian and explain why ill-conditioning forces a single-step-size trade-off between convergence speed in different directions.
  • Describe the structure of a linear program and explain why its optimum lies at a vertex of the feasible polytope.

5.1 Four Levels of ML Abstraction

When you write a large computer program, you have learned—usually the hard way—to break it down into modules with well-defined interfaces. If those abstraction barriers blur, the program becomes unmanageable. The same discipline applies to learning machine learning: at any moment you should know exactly which of four conceptual levels you are operating on. Conflating them leads to the kind of confusion where a derivation about an optimization algorithm is mistaken for a derivation about a model, or vice versa.

The four levels, from top to bottom, are: application and data, model and features, optimization problem, and optimization algorithm. They form a strict hierarchy: a change at any level almost certainly forces changes at every level below it. Recognizing this dependency saves enormous time when you need to swap out one component of a machine learning pipeline.

In this course, CS 189/289A, we focus primarily on the middle two levels—how to build a model and how to formulate the resulting optimization problem. We will study the bottom level (optimization algorithms) enough to be fluent users of existing software; the top level (application design and data collection) is touched throughout but could fill its own course.

5.1.1 Application and Data

Definition · Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning Tasks

A supervised learning task provides labeled training pairs $\{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ with $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$. When $y_i$ takes values in a discrete set $\mathcal{Y}$, the task is classification; when $y_i \in \mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{R}^k$), it is regression. An unsupervised learning task provides unlabeled data $\{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^n$; the goal is to discover structure. The two primary unsupervised tasks are clustering—partitioning points into groups of similar items—and dimensionality reduction—finding low-dimensional representations that preserve the geometry of the data.

The application level forces the most consequential decision in any ML project: what is the label set, and does it even exist? A self-driving car must both decide when to brake (classification: binary) and decide how hard to brake (regression: continuous force). These are separate sub-problems requiring separate models, even though both use the same sensor data as input. Confusing them—treating a regression problem as a classification problem, or vice versa—almost always produces poor results regardless of the sophistication of the model chosen.

Intuition · Why Clustering and Dimensionality Reduction Differ

Both are unsupervised, but they answer different questions. Clustering asks: are these points more similar to each other than to those points? The answer is a partition into discrete groups, like $k$-means. Dimensionality reduction asks: how is this data arranged along continuous axes of variation? Principal Components Analysis (PCA) answers this by finding the directions of maximum variance. The distinction matters for algorithm choice: if you need to assign new points to groups, use clustering; if you need to compress or visualize continuous structure, use dimensionality reduction.

5.1.2 Model, Features, and Capacity

Once the task is clear, the next decision is the model—the class of functions the algorithm is allowed to fit. Models span a vast range: linear classifiers, polynomial classifiers, logistic regression, decision trees, nearest neighbors, and neural networks all represent different hypotheses about what functions can generate the observed data. Feature engineering—choosing and transforming the raw inputs $\mathbf{x}_i$—is part of this level and is often more impactful than algorithm selection.

Definition · Model Capacity

Capacity is an informal measure of the complexity of the function class a model can represent—equivalently, how flexibly it can fit training data. As capacity increases, a model can bend its decision boundary (or regression surface) more intricately. Formally, capacity can be quantified by the Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension or Rademacher complexity, but informally it scales with the number of free parameters: a degree-$p$ polynomial has higher capacity than a linear function, and a neural network with more layers and wider layers has higher capacity than one with fewer.

Capacity is the lever that controls the overfitting-underfitting trade-off. Too little capacity and the model cannot capture the true structure of the data (underfitting, high bias). Too much capacity and the model memorizes training noise rather than learning generalizable patterns (overfitting, high variance). The right capacity is not fixed—it depends on the amount of training data, the noise level, and the complexity of the true underlying function.

Data Science Application · Feature Engineering in Practice

Professor Andrew Ng has observed that in real consulting engagements, roughly 70% of effort goes into feature engineering rather than algorithm selection or hyperparameter tuning. For a fraud-detection model, raw features might include transaction amount and merchant category, but engineered features—such as "number of transactions in this zip code in the last hour" or "deviation from the user's historical spending pattern"—encode domain knowledge that no algorithm can infer from raw data alone. Neural networks reduce (but do not eliminate) the need for manual feature engineering by learning features from raw inputs; on many standard benchmarks they outperform hand-engineered pipelines, but on structured or small-data problems, careful feature engineering frequently wins.

5.1.3 Optimization Problem and Algorithm

Most machine learning models ultimately express their training objective as an optimization problem: find the parameters $\mathbf{w}^*$ that minimize (or maximize) some objective function subject to constraints. The choice of objective function and constraints is the third level; the numerical procedure used to solve it is the fourth.

Definition · Optimization Problem Structure

A generic optimization problem has the form: $$\mathbf{w}^* = \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{\mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{W}} \; f(\mathbf{w}) \quad \text{subject to} \quad g_i(\mathbf{w}) \leq 0, \; i=1,\ldots,m,$$ where $f:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ is the objective function, $\mathcal{W} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is the feasible set, and $g_i$ are constraint functions. When $m=0$ (no constraints) the problem is unconstrained. When $f$ and all $g_i$ are linear, the problem is a linear program (LP). When $f$ is quadratic and the $g_i$ are linear, it is a quadratic program (QP).

Figure 5.1. The four levels of machine learning abstraction, from highest to lowest. Each layer sits on top of the one below it: the application determines what data is needed, the data shapes the model choice, the model determines what optimization problem arises, and the problem determines which optimization algorithm is appropriate. Critical rule: changing any layer forces re-examination of every layer below it. Color coding matches the design system: navy (application), blue (model), gold (optimization problem), green (algorithm).
💡
Key insight: In real-world ML projects, the most impactful improvements often come from the model and features level—tailoring representations to the structure of the data—rather than from switching optimization algorithms or tuning hyperparameters. Spend time here before diving into algorithmic complexity.
Warning · Context Switching Without Signaling

When reading textbooks or listening to lectures, the level of abstraction being discussed can shift without warning—from deriving a model to describing an optimization algorithm to interpreting an application result, sometimes within the same paragraph. Train yourself to ask at each step: "Are we defining the model, formulating the problem, or describing the algorithm?" Keeping these separate in your mind prevents a common source of confusion where a result about the algorithm (e.g., convergence rate) is incorrectly applied to a claim about the model (e.g., generalization).

5.2 Unconstrained Optimization

Once a model and objective function have been chosen, we face the optimization problem. The simplest case—and the most common starting point—is unconstrained optimization: no restrictions on which parameter vectors $\mathbf{w}$ are permitted. The perceptron of Chapter 1 is an example: its risk function was minimized over all of $\mathbb{R}^d$ with no constraints. The support vector machine, by contrast, introduces explicit constraints and becomes a quadratic program.

For unconstrained optimization to be tractable, we need to understand the geometry of the objective function. Two properties matter most: smoothness (does a gradient exist everywhere?) and convexity (does the function curve upward in all directions?). Smooth convex functions are the most amenable to optimization; every local minimum is a global minimum, and gradient descent is guaranteed to find it.

5.2.1 Objective Functions, Smoothness, and Minima

Definition · Smooth Objective Function, Global and Local Minima

An objective function is a function $f : \mathcal{W} \to \mathbb{R}$ to be minimized, where the domain $\mathcal{W} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ is the set of permitted parameter vectors. We call $f$ smooth if its gradient $\nabla f(\mathbf{w})$ exists and is continuous everywhere on $\mathcal{W}$.

A point $\mathbf{w}^* \in \mathcal{W}$ is a global minimizer of $f$ if $f(\mathbf{w}^*) \leq f(\mathbf{v})$ for all $\mathbf{v} \in \mathcal{W}$. It is a local minimizer if there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $f(\mathbf{w}^*) \leq f(\mathbf{v})$ for all $\mathbf{v} \in \mathcal{W}$ with $\|\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{w}^*\| < \delta$. Every global minimizer is a local minimizer, but not vice versa.

The distinction between global and local minimizers is the central difficulty of non-convex optimization. Finding a local minimizer is often tractable—just walk downhill until you stop. Finding the global minimizer may be NP-hard in the worst case. Fortunately, for the most important special case—convex functions—every local minimizer is automatically global.

5.2.2 Convex Functions: Definition and Properties

Convexity is the single most important structural property an objective function can have. When $f$ is convex, gradient descent is guaranteed to find the global minimum, and we can reason precisely about how fast it converges. Many fundamental ML objectives are convex: the perceptron loss, logistic regression loss, and the SVM hinge loss are all sums of convex functions, which are convex by the following key fact.

Definition · Convex Function

A function $f : \mathcal{W} \to \mathbb{R}$ defined on a convex set $\mathcal{W}$ (i.e., for all $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{W}$ and $\beta \in [0,1]$, $\mathbf{x} + \beta(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}) \in \mathcal{W}$) is convex if for every $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{W}$ and every $\beta \in [0,1]$: $$f\bigl(\mathbf{x} + \beta(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x})\bigr) \;\leq\; f(\mathbf{x}) + \beta\bigl(f(\mathbf{y}) - f(\mathbf{x})\bigr).$$ Equivalently, the chord connecting any two points on the graph of $f$ lies on or above the graph. A function $f$ is concave if $-f$ is convex.

The formal inequality says: if we interpolate a fraction $\beta$ of the way from $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{y}$, the function value at that interpolated point is at most the same fraction of the way between $f(\mathbf{x})$ and $f(\mathbf{y})$. In other words, the function curves upward—or at worst, goes straight—and never dips below its own chord.

Theorem · Sum of Convex Functions Is Convex

If $f_1, f_2, \ldots, f_n : \mathcal{W} \to \mathbb{R}$ are convex functions and $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n \geq 0$, then $$f(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i f_i(\mathbf{w})$$ is also convex. In particular, the perceptron loss $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{i:\text{mis.}} \max(0, -y_i(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}_i + \alpha))$ is convex as a sum of convex ramp functions.

Proof

For any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{W}$ and $\beta \in [0,1]$, by convexity of each $f_i$: $$f_i(\mathbf{x}+\beta(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x})) \leq f_i(\mathbf{x}) + \beta(f_i(\mathbf{y})-f_i(\mathbf{x})).$$ Multiply by $\lambda_i \geq 0$ and sum over $i$: $$\sum_i \lambda_i f_i(\mathbf{x}+\beta(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x})) \leq \sum_i \lambda_i f_i(\mathbf{x}) + \beta\Bigl(\sum_i \lambda_i f_i(\mathbf{y}) - \sum_i \lambda_i f_i(\mathbf{x})\Bigr),$$ which is exactly the convexity condition for $f = \sum_i \lambda_i f_i$. □

Figure 5.2. Formal illustration of convexity. Left: the convex parabola $f(w)=w^2$. The gold dashed chord between two points on the graph lies at or above the blue curve. The green point on the curve is at $f(x+\beta(y-x))$; the red diamond is the corresponding chord value; the purple arrow shows that the curve is always below the chord. Right: a concave function $f(w)=-w^2+4$; here the chord (gold dashed) lies below the red curve, confirming that $-f$ is convex.
Theorem · Structure of Minima for Convex Functions

Let $f : \mathcal{W} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous and convex on a closed convex domain $\mathcal{W}$. Exactly one of the following holds:

  1. $f$ has no minimum (the infimum is $-\infty$ or is not attained).
  2. $f$ has exactly one local minimum, which is therefore the unique global minimum.
  3. $f$ has multiple local minima, all sharing the same function value $f^*$, and the set of all minimizers $\mathcal{W}^* = \{\mathbf{w} : f(\mathbf{w}) = f^*\}$ is a non-empty, closed, convex set.
In cases (2) and (3), every local minimum is a global minimum.

Proof Sketch

Suppose $\mathbf{w}_1$ and $\mathbf{w}_2$ are both local minima of convex $f$ with $f(\mathbf{w}_1) < f(\mathbf{w}_2)$. For $\beta \in (0,1)$, convexity gives $f(\mathbf{w}_1 + \beta(\mathbf{w}_2-\mathbf{w}_1)) \leq f(\mathbf{w}_1) + \beta(f(\mathbf{w}_2)-f(\mathbf{w}_1)) < f(\mathbf{w}_2)$. But for small $\beta$, the interpolated point is near $\mathbf{w}_2$, and $f$ is strictly less there than at $\mathbf{w}_2$—contradicting $\mathbf{w}_2$ being a local minimum. Hence all local minima have the same $f$-value. Convexity of the minimizer set $\mathcal{W}^*$ then follows directly from the definition of convexity applied to two minimizers. □

This theorem is the reason convexity matters so much in practice. In cases (2) and (3), any algorithm that walks downhill—including gradient descent—is guaranteed to reach the global optimum. For non-convex objectives like neural network losses, there may be exponentially many local minima at different function values, and gradient descent can get stuck in a bad one. The remarkable empirical finding for wide neural networks is that local minima tend to cluster near the global optimum, which partially explains why SGD works in practice despite non-convexity.

Figure 5.3. Three cases for minima of convex vs. non-convex functions. Left: convex parabola $f(w)=w^2+1$—unique global minimum; gold chord lies above blue curve. Center: convex piecewise-linear function with a flat minimum region (shaded gold)—multiple global minima forming a connected convex set, all with equal $f$-value. Right: non-convex quartic with two local minima (red dots), only one of which (gold star) is the global minimum—gradient descent starting near the left local minimum will get stuck there.
Example · Checking Convexity of the Hinge Loss

Setup. The SVM hinge loss for a single training point $(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)$ is $\ell_i(\mathbf{w}) = \max(0, 1 - y_i(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}_i))$.

Check. Both $g_1(\mathbf{w}) = 0$ and $g_2(\mathbf{w}) = 1 - y_i(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}_i)$ are convex (the first is constant; the second is affine, hence convex). The pointwise maximum of convex functions is convex: for any $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}$ and $\beta \in [0,1]$, $$\max(g_1, g_2)(\mathbf{u}+\beta(\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u})) \leq \max\bigl(g_1(\mathbf{u})+\beta(g_1(\mathbf{v})-g_1(\mathbf{u})),\, g_2(\mathbf{u})+\beta(g_2(\mathbf{v})-g_2(\mathbf{u}))\bigr)$$ by convexity of each $g_j$, and the max of these two is at most the chord of $\max(g_1,g_2)$.

Conclusion. The SVM objective $\sum_i \ell_i(\mathbf{w}) + \lambda\|\mathbf{w}\|^2$ is a sum of convex functions (by the sum theorem above) plus a strongly convex regularizer, giving a strictly convex overall objective. This guarantees a unique global minimum, which is why the SVM has an exact solution.

5.3 Gradient Descent

With an objective function in hand, we need an algorithm to minimize it. The most fundamental and widely used algorithm in machine learning is gradient descent: iteratively move the parameter vector in the direction opposite to the gradient of the objective function. This is the algorithmic backbone of nearly everything in the field, from the perceptron to GPT.

Despite its simplicity, gradient descent has important failure modes and tuning challenges. Chief among them is the choice of step size (also called the learning rate): too large and the algorithm may overshoot and diverge; too small and it converges so slowly that training becomes impractical. Understanding the step-size dynamics is the most important practical skill for applying gradient descent to real problems.

5.3.1 The Basic Algorithm

Definition · Gradient Descent

Given a smooth objective function $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$, a starting point $\mathbf{w}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^d$, and a step size (learning rate) $\varepsilon > 0$, the gradient descent algorithm produces the sequence: $$\mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \mathbf{w}_t - \varepsilon \nabla f(\mathbf{w}_t), \quad t = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$ until a stopping criterion is met (e.g., $\|\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_t)\| < \delta$ for some tolerance $\delta > 0$, or a fixed number of iterations).

The gradient $\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_t)$ points in the direction of steepest ascent of $f$ at $\mathbf{w}_t$. Subtracting it (scaled by $\varepsilon$) therefore moves us in the direction of steepest descent. For a convex function, this guarantees that $f(\mathbf{w}_{t+1}) \leq f(\mathbf{w}_t)$ as long as $\varepsilon$ is small enough—every step reduces the objective. For non-convex functions, the same inequality holds locally, but we may descend into a local minimum that is not global.

Gradient Descent Update
$$\mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \mathbf{w}_t - \varepsilon \, \nabla f(\mathbf{w}_t)$$

In practice, gradient descent almost never reaches the exact minimizer in finite steps—it converges asymptotically, getting ever closer but never arriving exactly. "Convergence" means the sequence $\{\mathbf{w}_t\}$ has a limit $\mathbf{w}^*$ with $\nabla f(\mathbf{w}^*) = 0$ (a critical point). For strictly convex functions, this critical point is the unique global minimizer.

5.3.2 Step-Size Effects: Divergence and Slow Convergence

The step size $\varepsilon$ is the most sensitive hyperparameter in gradient descent. The four panels of Figure 5.4 show gradient descent on the simple one-dimensional parabola $f(w) = w^2$: with $\varepsilon = 0.10$ the algorithm converges but slowly; with $\varepsilon = 0.48$ it converges in very few steps (close to optimal); with $\varepsilon = 0.95$ it oscillates; and with $\varepsilon = 1.01$ it diverges catastrophically.

Theorem · Convergence of Gradient Descent for Quadratic Objectives

Let $f(\mathbf{w}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{w}^\top H \mathbf{w}$ where $H$ is positive definite with smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\min} > 0$ and largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}$. Then gradient descent with constant step size $\varepsilon$ satisfies: $$f(\mathbf{w}_{t+1}) - f(\mathbf{w}^*) \leq \left(1 - 2\varepsilon\lambda_{\min} + \varepsilon^2 \lambda_{\max}^2\right) \bigl(f(\mathbf{w}_t) - f(\mathbf{w}^*)\bigr).$$ Convergence is guaranteed iff the contraction factor is less than 1, which requires $\varepsilon < 2/\lambda_{\max}$. The optimal step size is $\varepsilon^* = 1/\lambda_{\max}$, and the optimal convergence rate per step is $(1 - \lambda_{\min}/\lambda_{\max})$.

Proof Sketch

The update on the quadratic $f$ is linear: $\mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \mathbf{w}_t - \varepsilon H \mathbf{w}_t = (I - \varepsilon H)\mathbf{w}_t$. Since $H$ is diagonalizable (being symmetric positive definite), we can write $\mathbf{w}_t = Q\boldsymbol{\alpha}_t$ where $Q$ contains the eigenvectors of $H$. In this basis, each component $\alpha_{t,j}$ evolves as $\alpha_{t+1,j} = (1-\varepsilon\lambda_j)\alpha_{t,j}$, so after $t$ steps $\alpha_{t,j} = (1-\varepsilon\lambda_j)^t \alpha_{0,j}$. Convergence of component $j$ requires $|1-\varepsilon\lambda_j| < 1$, i.e., $0 < \varepsilon < 2/\lambda_j$. The most restrictive constraint comes from the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_{\max}$, giving $\varepsilon < 2/\lambda_{\max}$. □

Figure 5.4. Gradient descent on $f(w)=w^2$ starting at $w_0=2.5$, for 20 iterations with four step sizes. Top-left $\varepsilon=0.10$: converges but slowly (arrows stay green, path is long). Top-right $\varepsilon=0.48$: near-optimal, converges in very few steps. Bottom-left $\varepsilon=0.95$: overshoots repeatedly (oscillation) but still converges. Bottom-right $\varepsilon=1.01$: diverges—each step increases $f(w)$, shown by red points flying off the parabola. The red dashed vertical line marks the true minimum at $w^*=0$.
Warning · Choosing Step Size by Trial and Error

There is no universal "right" step size. For a perfect parabola, the optimal $\varepsilon = 1/(2\lambda_{\max})$ can be computed analytically, but for a neural network with a billion parameters and a non-quadratic, non-convex loss, $\lambda_{\max}$ is neither known nor constant across training. In practice: start with a small step size (e.g., $\varepsilon = 10^{-3}$), monitor the training loss, and double it until you see oscillation, then back off. For neural networks, this tuning can take hours and is a major practical burden.

5.3.3 Adaptive Learning Rates

The difficulty of choosing $\varepsilon$ motivates adaptive learning rate methods, which automatically adjust the step size during training. The simplest adaptation is the backtracking line search: after computing a proposed step, check whether $f$ actually decreased; if not, reject the step, halve $\varepsilon$, and try again. This prevents divergence at the cost of extra function evaluations.

Definition · Backtracking Line Search

Given current parameters $\mathbf{w}_t$ and descent direction $\mathbf{d}_t = -\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_t)$, the backtracking line search finds the step size $\varepsilon_t$ by the procedure:

  1. Initialize $\varepsilon_t = \varepsilon_0$ (some initial value).
  2. If $f(\mathbf{w}_t + \varepsilon_t \mathbf{d}_t) \geq f(\mathbf{w}_t)$, set $\varepsilon_t \leftarrow \varepsilon_t / 2$ and repeat.
  3. Accept the step: $\mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \mathbf{w}_t + \varepsilon_t \mathbf{d}_t$.
This guarantees $f(\mathbf{w}_{t+1}) < f(\mathbf{w}_t)$ at every step, preventing divergence for smooth $f$.

Beyond backtracking, modern deep learning uses per-parameter adaptive methods. The most widely deployed is Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation), which maintains running estimates of the first and second moments of the gradient for each parameter, and uses these to assign an effective step size to each parameter dimension. For the ill-conditioned objective functions typical in deep learning, Adam dramatically outperforms fixed-step-size gradient descent. We return to these methods in the neural network chapters.

Data Science Application · Learning Rate Schedules in Deep Learning

Training large language models (LLMs) like GPT-3 requires carefully designed learning rate schedules. A typical schedule warms up from a near-zero learning rate to a peak value over the first few thousand steps (to avoid instability from random initialization), holds constant during the bulk of training, then decays (often as $1/\sqrt{t}$ or via cosine annealing) toward zero. The Chinchilla scaling laws showed that, for a fixed compute budget, the optimal approach is to jointly optimize model size, dataset size, and learning rate schedule—not just model size alone. The adaptive method Adam with $\beta_1=0.9$, $\beta_2=0.999$ is the near-universal default for transformer models.

5.4 Conditioning and 2D Gradient Descent

Moving from one dimension to multiple dimensions reveals a new failure mode of gradient descent that cannot arise in 1D: ill-conditioning. Even when a single step size is small enough to prevent divergence in every direction, the optimal step size differs by direction. The direction that most prefers a small step forces all other directions to slow down to that pace—a global bottleneck set by the "worst" direction.

The degree of this mismatch is quantified by the condition number of the Hessian matrix, the ratio of its largest to smallest eigenvalue. A condition number near 1 means all directions behave similarly (well-conditioned); a large condition number means some directions want a much smaller step than others (ill-conditioned). In deep learning, condition numbers can be in the millions, making naive gradient descent essentially useless without adaptive methods.

5.4.1 Hessian Matrix and Condition Number

Definition · Hessian Matrix

For a twice-differentiable function $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$, the Hessian matrix at $\mathbf{w}$ is the $d\times d$ symmetric matrix of second partial derivatives: $$H(\mathbf{w}) = \nabla^2 f(\mathbf{w}) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial w_1^2} & \cdots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial w_1 \partial w_d} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial w_d \partial w_1} & \cdots & \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial w_d^2} \end{pmatrix}.$$ The Hessian is the multivariate generalization of the second derivative. For a quadratic $f(\mathbf{w}) = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{w}^\top H \mathbf{w}$, the Hessian is constant and equals $H$. The eigenvalues of $H$ determine the curvature of $f$ in each principal direction: a large eigenvalue means high curvature (steep bowl) and a small eigenvalue means low curvature (shallow slope).

Definition · Condition Number

For a symmetric positive definite matrix $H$ with eigenvalues $0 < \lambda_{\min} \leq \cdots \leq \lambda_{\max}$, the condition number is: $$\kappa(H) = \frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}}.$$ A matrix is well-conditioned if $\kappa(H) \approx 1$ (level sets of $\mathbf{w}^\top H \mathbf{w}$ are near-circular); ill-conditioned if $\kappa(H) \gg 1$ (level sets are elongated ellipsoids). The optimal step size for gradient descent on $f$ is $\varepsilon^* = 1/\lambda_{\max}$, and after this choice the convergence rate in the direction of $\lambda_{\min}$ is $(1-1/\kappa)$—slow when $\kappa$ is large.

Figure 5.5. Isocontours of $f(\mathbf{w}) = a w_1^2 + b w_2^2$ for two cases. Left: well-conditioned ($a=b=1$, $\kappa=1$)—circular contours; any reasonable step size works equally in all directions. Right: ill-conditioned ($a=10$, $b=1$, $\kappa=10$)—elongated ellipses; the step size that avoids divergence in the $w_1$ direction ($\varepsilon < 1/20$) is 10$\times$ smaller than the step size optimal for the $w_2$ direction. The red star marks the global minimum at the origin in both cases.

5.4.2 Ill-Conditioning in Practice

Figure 5.6 makes the trade-off concrete across three scenarios: a well-conditioned problem converges quickly with a moderate step size; the same step size causes divergence on an ill-conditioned problem; reducing the step size prevents divergence but dramatically slows convergence in the easy direction. This is not a pathological edge case—it is the generic behavior of gradient descent on realistic ML objectives.

Figure 5.6. Gradient descent (20 iterations, gold path) on two quadratic objectives. Left: $f=2w_1^2+w_2^2$, $\varepsilon=0.105$—converges to the origin (navy star) in well under 20 steps; start (green dot) and end (red X) nearly coincide with the optimum. Center: $f=10w_1^2+w_2^2$, same $\varepsilon$—diverges; the path spirals outward because $\varepsilon > 2/\lambda_{\max}=0.1$ in the $w_1$ direction. Right: same ill-conditioned function but $\varepsilon=0.055$—no longer diverges, but after 20 steps the path is still far from the origin in the $w_2$ direction, illustrating the slow-convergence cost of reducing $\varepsilon$.
Intuition · Why Ill-Conditioning Causes a Dilemma

Imagine a narrow valley in a landscape. The valley walls are steep (high curvature, large eigenvalue) and the valley floor slopes gently toward the exit (low curvature, small eigenvalue). To avoid bouncing off the steep walls, you must take tiny steps. But tiny steps also mean you inch along the gently-sloping floor, taking a million steps to get where a larger step could have taken you in ten. The only solution is to take different-sized steps in different directions—exactly what adaptive methods like Adam do by estimating per-parameter curvature from gradient history.

Example · Computing the Condition Number for Least Squares

Setup. In ordinary least squares regression, the objective is $f(\boldsymbol{\beta}) = \|X\boldsymbol{\beta} - \mathbf{y}\|^2$, where $X$ is an $n\times d$ design matrix. The Hessian is $H = 2X^\top X$.

Condition number. $\kappa(H) = \lambda_{\max}(X^\top X)/\lambda_{\min}(X^\top X) = \sigma_{\max}^2(X)/\sigma_{\min}^2(X)$, where $\sigma_{\max}$ and $\sigma_{\min}$ are the largest and smallest singular values of $X$.

Interpretation. If two features are nearly collinear (one is almost a linear combination of the other), $X^\top X$ has a near-zero eigenvalue, making $\kappa$ enormous. This is the classical multicollinearity problem in statistics. Gradient descent on such data will be extremely slow; ridge regression (adding $\lambda I$ to $X^\top X$) increases $\lambda_{\min}$ to at least $\lambda$, capping $\kappa \leq (\lambda_{\max}+\lambda)/\lambda$ and making the problem well-conditioned. This is one of several reasons why regularization is useful beyond preventing overfitting.

ℹ️
Connection to SVMs: The quadratic program for the SVM (Chapter 3) involves the Gram matrix $K_{ij} = \mathbf{x}_i \cdot \mathbf{x}_j$. If the data features are poorly scaled, this matrix is ill-conditioned, and the QP solver (which is a more sophisticated optimization algorithm than gradient descent) will also struggle. Normalizing features before running the SVM is essential for both numerical stability and optimization speed.

5.5 Linear Programs

Gradient descent is the workhorse of unconstrained (and lightly constrained) optimization. But many important ML problems have hard inequality constraints—requirements that the solution must satisfy regardless of the objective. The simplest such structure is a linear program (LP): a linear objective subject to linear inequality constraints. Linear programs are ubiquitous in operations research, economics, and combinatorics, but they also appear in machine learning: the hard-margin SVM can be reformulated as an LP, and certain robust regression problems have LP structure.

The key insight about linear programs is geometric: the feasible region (the set of $\mathbf{w}$ satisfying all constraints) is a convex polytope—a higher-dimensional generalization of a polygon. The objective function $c^\top \mathbf{w}$ defines a family of parallel hyperplanes; its maximum over the polytope is attained at one of the polytope’s vertices (corners). This means we do not need calculus—we only need to evaluate the objective at finitely many vertices, or use the Simplex algorithm to navigate the vertices efficiently.

5.5.1 Standard Form and Feasible Polytope

Definition · Linear Program (Standard Inequality Form)

A linear program in $d$ variables $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is an optimization problem of the form: $$\operatorname*{maximize}_{\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d} \; \mathbf{c}^\top \mathbf{w} \quad \text{subject to} \quad A\mathbf{w} \leq \mathbf{b},$$ where $\mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is the cost vector, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ is the constraint matrix, and $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^m$ is the right-hand-side vector. The inequality $A\mathbf{w} \leq \mathbf{b}$ is interpreted component-wise: $\mathbf{a}_i^\top \mathbf{w} \leq b_i$ for each row $i = 1,\ldots,m$. The feasible region $\mathcal{P} = \{\mathbf{w} : A\mathbf{w} \leq \mathbf{b}\}$ is a convex polytope (possibly unbounded). Minimization is equivalent: minimize $\mathbf{c}^\top \mathbf{w}$ iff maximize $(-\mathbf{c})^\top \mathbf{w}$.

In the ML context, $m$ often equals $n$ (one constraint per training point), $d$ is the feature dimension, each row $\mathbf{a}_i$ encodes a constraint imposed by training point $\mathbf{x}_i$, and $b_i$ encodes the corresponding margin or label requirement. The fact that the constraint matrix comes directly from the training data is what makes LP-based classifiers interpretable and certifiable: every constraint has a clear meaning.

5.5.2 The Vertex Optimality Theorem

Theorem · Linear Objective Optimum at a Vertex

Let $\mathcal{P} = \{\mathbf{w} : A\mathbf{w} \leq \mathbf{b}\}$ be a bounded, non-empty convex polytope. Then for any linear objective $f(\mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{c}^\top \mathbf{w}$, there exists a vertex (extreme point) $\mathbf{v}$ of $\mathcal{P}$ such that $\mathbf{c}^\top \mathbf{v} = \max_{\mathbf{w} \in \mathcal{P}} \mathbf{c}^\top \mathbf{w}$.

Proof

Let $\mathbf{w}^*$ be any maximizer of $f$ on $\mathcal{P}$. If $\mathbf{w}^*$ is not a vertex, then by definition there exist $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in \mathcal{P}$ and $\lambda \in (0,1)$ such that $\mathbf{w}^* = \lambda \mathbf{u} + (1-\lambda)\mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{u} \neq \mathbf{v}$. Then $\mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{w}^* = \lambda(\mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{u}) + (1-\lambda)(\mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{v})$. Since $\mathbf{w}^*$ is a maximizer, $\mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{u} \leq \mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{w}^*$ and $\mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{v} \leq \mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{w}^*$. If either inequality is strict, then the convex combination is strictly less than $\mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{w}^*$, a contradiction. Hence $\mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{w}^*$; both $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are also maximizers. Repeating this argument (the polytope has finitely many vertices), we eventually reach a vertex maximizer. □

This theorem is the foundation of the Simplex algorithm: start at any vertex of $\mathcal{P}$, move to an adjacent vertex that improves the objective, repeat until no adjacent vertex is better. Since the polytope has finitely many vertices and the objective increases at each step, the algorithm terminates. In the worst case, the Simplex algorithm is exponential, but in practice it runs in polynomial time on virtually all real LP instances.

Figure 5.7. A two-dimensional linear program: maximize $\mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{w} = w_1 + 2w_2$ subject to $w_1+w_2\leq 4$ (blue dashed), $2w_1+w_2\leq 6$ (green dashed), $w_1\geq 0$, $w_2\geq 0$ (teal dotted). The feasible region (blue polygon) has four vertices (red dots). The gold iso-objective lines $c^\top\mathbf{w}=\text{const}$ sweep from lower-left to upper-right; the objective is maximized at the vertex $(2,2)$ (navy star), where $c^\top\mathbf{w}=6$—no other feasible point achieves a higher value. The Simplex algorithm would navigate from $(0,0)$ to $(0,4)$ or $(3,0)$, then to $(2,2)$ by following improving edges of the polytope.
Example · LP Formulation for a Hard-Margin Classifier

Setup. Given linearly separable training data $\{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}$ with $y_i \in \{-1,+1\}$, we want to find $\mathbf{w}$ such that $y_i(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}_i) \geq 1$ for all $i$. To minimize $\|\mathbf{w}\|_1 = \sum_j |w_j|$ (a sparsity-inducing objective), we introduce variables $t_j \geq 0$ such that $t_j \geq w_j$ and $t_j \geq -w_j$ for each $j$.

LP form. Variables: $(\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{t}) \in \mathbb{R}^{2d}$. Objective: minimize $\sum_j t_j$ (linear in $\mathbf{t}$). Constraints: $y_i(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}_i) \geq 1$ for $i=1,\ldots,n$; $t_j \geq w_j$ and $t_j \geq -w_j$ for $j=1,\ldots,d$. All constraints are linear inequalities. This LP has $2d$ variables and $n+2d$ constraints and can be solved in polynomial time by interior-point methods.

Significance. Minimizing $\|\mathbf{w}\|_1$ rather than $\|\mathbf{w}\|_2$ encourages sparsity—many weights are driven exactly to zero—making the resulting classifier interpretable. This is the Lasso principle applied to classification.

Data Science Application · Linear Programs in Operations Research and ML

LP solvers underlie a remarkable range of applications. In supply-chain optimization, an LP finds the minimum-cost allocation of goods across warehouses subject to supply, demand, and capacity constraints. In network routing, an LP finds minimum-latency paths subject to bandwidth constraints. In machine learning, the Wasserstein distance between two probability distributions—used in optimal transport and generative modeling—is the solution to an LP. The dual of the hard-margin SVM (which we studied as a QP) can also be reformulated as an LP in certain special cases. Modern LP solvers (e.g., Gurobi, CPLEX) can handle millions of variables and constraints in seconds.

✦ Chapter Summary

This chapter established the conceptual architecture of machine learning as a four-level hierarchy: application and data determine the task and label structure; model and features determine the hypothesis class and capacity; optimization problem translates the model into a formal mathematical objective with constraints; and optimization algorithm produces a numerical solution. Changes cascade downward through this hierarchy. The chapter then developed the mathematical tools for the bottom two levels: the theory of convex functions, which guarantees that gradient descent finds global optima; the dynamics of gradient descent under varying step sizes; the condition number as a quantitative measure of gradient-descent difficulty; and the structure of linear programs as a foundational example of constrained optimization.

FOUR ABSTRACTION LEVELS

Application/data, model/features, optimization problem, optimization algorithm form a strict hierarchy. A change at any level forces redesign of all levels below. Most of this course focuses on the middle two. Recognizing which level you are on at any moment is essential for clear thinking.

CLASSIFICATION VS. REGRESSION

Classification maps $\mathbf{x} \to$ discrete label; regression maps $\mathbf{x} \to$ continuous value. Clustering (unsupervised) groups unlabeled data; dimensionality reduction (unsupervised) finds low-dimensional representations. The correct task type must be identified before choosing a model.

MODEL CAPACITY

Capacity measures how flexibly a model can fit data; it scales roughly with the number of parameters. Too little capacity $\Rightarrow$ underfitting (high bias); too much $\Rightarrow$ overfitting (high variance). Diagnosing overfitting or underfitting drives capacity selection in practice.

CONVEX FUNCTIONS

$f$ is convex iff for all $\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}$ and $\beta\in[0,1]$: $f(\mathbf{x}+\beta(\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}))\leq f(\mathbf{x})+\beta(f(\mathbf{y})-f(\mathbf{x}))$. Sums of convex functions are convex. A continuous convex function on a closed convex domain has either no minimum, a unique global minimum, or a convex set of global minima—all with equal value.

GLOBAL VS. LOCAL MINIMA

Every global minimizer is a local minimizer; for convex $f$, every local minimizer is global. Non-convex functions (e.g., deep network losses) may have exponentially many local minima at different values. Wide neural networks empirically exhibit local minima nearly as good as global, explaining why SGD works.

GRADIENT DESCENT

Update: $\mathbf{w}_{t+1} = \mathbf{w}_t - \varepsilon\nabla f(\mathbf{w}_t)$. Converges for quadratic $f$ iff $\varepsilon < 2/\lambda_{\max}$. Optimal step: $\varepsilon^* = 1/\lambda_{\max}$. Too large $\Rightarrow$ divergence; too small $\Rightarrow$ slow convergence. Backtracking line search prevents divergence adaptively.

HESSIAN AND CONDITIONING

The Hessian $H = \nabla^2 f$ is the matrix of second derivatives. Its eigenvalues give per-direction curvature. Condition number $\kappa = \lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}$: large $\kappa$ means elongated ellipsoidal level sets and a single step size cannot be optimal in all directions. Adaptive methods (Adam) address this.

ILL-CONDITIONING IN ML

Nearly collinear features give $X^\top X$ a near-zero eigenvalue and huge condition number. Ridge regression (adding $\lambda I$) caps $\kappa\leq(\lambda_{\max}+\lambda)/\lambda$. Feature normalization before training reduces ill-conditioning. Neural networks typically have large $\kappa$, making Adam the practical default over plain SGD.

LINEAR PROGRAMS

Standard form: maximize $\mathbf{c}^\top\mathbf{w}$ subject to $A\mathbf{w}\leq\mathbf{b}$. The feasible region is a convex polytope. By the vertex optimality theorem, the LP optimum is always attained at a vertex. The Simplex algorithm navigates vertices; interior-point methods solve LPs in polynomial time.

ADAPTIVE LEARNING RATES

Backtracking line search: after each step, if $f$ increased, halve $\varepsilon$ and retry. Adam: maintains per-parameter estimates of gradient mean and variance, scaling each update by $1/\sqrt{\hat{v}}$ to equalize effective step sizes. Used universally in deep learning. Learning rate schedules (warmup + decay) further improve training stability.

Exercises

Exercise 5.1  ·  FOUR ABSTRACTION LEVELS
Mapping a Fraud Detection Pipeline to the Four Levels

A bank wants to flag fraudulent credit card transactions in real time. Each transaction has 30 features (amount, merchant category, time of day, etc.). The bank has 500,000 labeled historical transactions (fraud/not-fraud) and 10,000 new unlabeled transactions per day.

  1. Application level. Identify the task type (classification vs. regression vs. clustering), the label set $\mathcal{Y}$, and one key challenge at this level (e.g., class imbalance, concept drift, latency constraints).
  2. Model level. Propose two different models with different capacities for this problem. For each, describe what hypothesis class it represents and whether you expect it to underfit or overfit given $n=500{,}000$ training points.
  3. Optimization problem level. Write the optimization problem for logistic regression on this data—give the objective function and any constraints. Is this a convex problem? Is it constrained or unconstrained?
  4. Cascade principle. The bank decides to change from logistic regression to a neural network (changing the model level). What must change at the optimization problem level (objective function, constraints, structure) and at the optimization algorithm level? Justify each change.
Exercise 5.2  ·  CONVEXITY
Verifying Convexity for Common ML Loss Functions

For each function below, determine whether it is convex, concave, or neither, and prove your claim.

  1. Squared loss. $f(w) = (w - y)^2$ for fixed $y \in \mathbb{R}$, $w \in \mathbb{R}$. Use the formal definition (not calculus).
  2. Cross-entropy loss. $f(w) = -y\log\sigma(w) - (1-y)\log(1-\sigma(w))$ where $\sigma(w) = 1/(1+e^{-w})$ and $y \in \{0,1\}$ is fixed. Compute $f''(w)$ and determine the sign.
  3. Perceptron risk. Show that $\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{i=1}^n \max(0, -y_i(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}_i))$ is convex using the theorem that sums of convex functions are convex. You must verify that each summand is convex.
  4. Data science implication. For a function that is convex, what does this guarantee about gradient descent? For a function that is non-convex, what additional difficulty arises, and name one practical technique that helps address it?
Exercise 5.3  ·  GRADIENT DESCENT STEP SIZE
Diagnosing Step-Size Pathologies in Neural Network Training

You are training a small neural network and observe the following training loss curves over 100 epochs. Assume the loss is locally well-approximated by $f(w) = \frac{1}{2}hw^2$ with $h > 0$ near the minimum.

  1. Divergence condition. Derive the condition on $\varepsilon$ (in terms of $h$) for gradient descent to diverge on $f(w) = \frac{1}{2}hw^2$. Show that if $\varepsilon > 2/h$, the iterates $\{w_t\}$ are unbounded.
  2. Optimal step size. Find the step size $\varepsilon^*$ that minimizes the number of steps to reach $|w_t| < \delta$ from $w_0 = 1$. Express the number of steps as a function of $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$, then minimize over $\varepsilon \in (0, 2/h)$.
  3. Practical diagnosis. In your neural network training, the loss decreases for the first 10 epochs, then suddenly spikes upward and oscillates. What is the most likely cause, and what would you do to fix it?
  4. Adam vs. SGD. Explain in one paragraph why Adam typically outperforms vanilla gradient descent on ill-conditioned neural network losses. Specifically, how does Adam’s per-parameter step size address the condition-number problem described in Section 5.4?
Exercise 5.4  ·  HESSIAN AND CONDITIONING
Feature Scaling and Condition Numbers in Polynomial Regression

You are fitting a degree-2 polynomial to $n=100$ data points: $\hat{y} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2$, where $x$ is age in years, ranging from 1 to 100. The design matrix is $X \in \mathbb{R}^{100 \times 3}$ with columns $[1, x_i, x_i^2]$.

  1. Condition number. Without computing explicitly, argue why $\kappa(X^\top X)$ is very large. What is the relationship between the magnitudes of columns 2 and 3 of $X$, and how does this affect the eigenvalues of $X^\top X$?
  2. Effect on gradient descent. Given that $\kappa(X^\top X) \approx 10^6$ for the raw features, what is the ratio of the optimal step sizes for the fastest and slowest converging directions? What does this mean for gradient descent convergence speed?
  3. Remedy. Describe two approaches to reduce $\kappa(X^\top X)$: (i) standardizing features (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation), and (ii) adding ridge regularization. For each, explain why and how it reduces $\kappa$.
  4. Data science connection. In a neural network with input features of vastly different scales (pixel intensities 0–255 mixed with binary indicators 0/1), what is the effect on the Hessian and training speed? What preprocessing step is universally recommended, and why?
Exercise 5.5  ·  LINEAR PROGRAMS
Optimal Resource Allocation for a Machine Learning Training Cluster

A cloud computing cluster has $G=8$ GPUs and $M=32$ GB of RAM. Two job types compete for resources: training job A uses 2 GPUs and 4 GB RAM per instance, yields a score of 3; training job B uses 1 GPU and 6 GB RAM per instance, yields a score of 5. Let $w_1, w_2 \geq 0$ be the number of instances of each job to run simultaneously.

  1. LP formulation. Write the linear program to maximize total score. Identify $\mathbf{c}$, $A$, and $\mathbf{b}$ explicitly. How many variables and constraints does the LP have?
  2. Geometric solution. Draw the feasible region in the $(w_1, w_2)$ plane. Label all vertices. Evaluate the objective at each vertex and identify the optimal solution.
  3. Vertex optimality. The Vertex Optimality Theorem guarantees the optimum is at a vertex. Give an intuitive explanation of why a non-vertex interior point cannot be optimal for a linear objective over a convex polytope.
  4. Sensitivity analysis. If the score for job B increases from 5 to 8, does the optimal solution change? Recompute. More generally, for what range of scores $s_B$ (with $s_A=3$ fixed) does the original vertex remain optimal?
